name: Apinaye
confidence_why: Oliveira 2005's reference grammar and Callow 1962's thesis independently put main stress on the final syllable, Salanova 2001 agrees once epenthetic echo vowels are set aside, and the dissent of Ham 1961 (stress called phonemic, several per rhythm group) and Albuquerque 2007 (stress on one of the last two syllables, mostly the last) comes from briefer, weaker descriptions whose own examples show every root stressed on its last true syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog (StressTyp2) records fixed final stress. Ham does not state a placement rule; she calls stress phonemic (contrastive) and reports several stresses per word, which is a claim of a different type. Her contrast examples, however, are rhythm groups made of several roots each bearing its own stress, and every root in her data is stressed on its last non-echo syllable, so the data are compatible with final stress at the root level with echo vowels outside the stress domain.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ham treats stress as a phoneme: stressed and unstressed syllables contrast, and a rhythm group (roughly a word) can carry more than one stress; she gives no placement rule. Stress is listed as an addition relative to Callow's earlier paper. Her transcriptions throughout put the stress mark on the last non-echo syllable of each root (e.g. a'tšəva͜A 'your tooth', aya'kəva͜A 'your mouth', ga'põ 'searched', ka'tut 'shoulder'), and compounds/phrases get one stress per root ('tεb'radž͜i 'big fish', 'tšũ'rε 'name'); the word-final release/echo vowels (written ͜A, ͜I etc.) are unstressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; several full stresses per rhythm group are noted (p. 33). Stress at 'foot level' conditions stop voicing (voiceless stops voice in unstressed non-initial syllables, p. 28) and the [y]/[ž̯] allophony of /z/ (p. 4).
new_statements.exceptions: ['kəṛ̌agri] 'beneath' is transcribed with initial stress only; [ka'tu·'di͜I] 'shoulder' beside [ka'tut͜U] shows the echo-vowel variant carrying its own stress. Long consonants 'fluctuate freely when stressed' (p. 5).
new_statements.identity_note: Ham 1961: data gathered 1959-1961 in the northern tip of Goiás (now Tocantins) from two women about 20 years old, ~60% bilingual in Portuguese; the 2009 SIL archive edition is an edited re-typing of the 1961 Arquivo Linguístico No. 106 paper. Salanova 2001: Apinayé data from one speaker (Kangroti Apinayé); the thesis covers Mebengokre (Kayapó and Xikrin dialects) and Apinayé together, and the p. 21 and p. 24 stress remarks are about Mebengokre, not Apinayé.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's final stress: the tonic syllable is the last syllable of the underlying root, with the epenthetic echo vowel that makes citation forms surface-paroxytone outside the count, and clitic-like particles unstressed. The explicit 'underlyingly final' statement (p. 21) is made for Mebengokre, not Apinayé; for Apinayé the placement is inferred from the transcribed examples and the strong/weak-syllable equation.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No explicit stress rule for Apinayé is given; the thesis is about nasality. What it shows is that the stressed syllable is the last underlying syllable of the lexical root (the word-final epenthetic echo vowel is unstressed: [ˈrɔbɔ], [ˈʌgʌ], [ˈtono], [pi.jaˈʌ.mʌ] 'shame' p. 77), that grammatical particles (pronouns, tense/aspect markers, exclamations) 'não possuem acento próprio' (have no stress of their own, p. 33), and that unstressed vowels do not contrast in nasality (p. 77). For the sister language Mebengokre it states outright that the tonic syllable is 'subjacentemente final' (underlyingly final, p. 21) and that surface paroxytones arise only through epenthesis.
new_statements.exceptions: Ex. (98d) /pʌ̃m/ [pʌ̃ˈmʌ] 'father' (p. 77) is transcribed with the stress on the epenthetic echo syllable, unlike the other epenthesis examples; particles are unaccented and undergo vowel syncope/reduction (p. 33, and p. 14 for Xikrin Mebengokre).
new_statements.identity_note: Ham 1961: data gathered 1959-1961 in the northern tip of Goiás (now Tocantins) from two women about 20 years old, ~60% bilingual in Portuguese; the 2009 SIL archive edition is an edited re-typing of the 1961 Arquivo Linguístico No. 106 paper. Salanova 2001: Apinayé data from one speaker (Kangroti Apinayé); the thesis covers Mebengokre (Kayapó and Xikrin dialects) and Apinayé together, and the p. 21 and p. 24 stress remarks are about Mebengokre, not Apinayé.

readall_conflicts: One disagreement of type rather than placement: Ham (1961, p. 33) calls Apinayé stress phonemic ('There is contrast between stressed syllables and non-stressed syllables'; 'Phonemic stress' listed as an addition to Callow) and notes that a rhythm group ('word') can carry several stresses, whereas the catalog (StressTyp2) records fixed final stress and Salanova (2001) treats the tonic syllable as the last underlying syllable of the root with unstressed epenthetic echo vowels and unaccented particles. The two are reconcilable if the stress domain is the root/morpheme rather than the phonological word: Ham's contrast pairs are multi-root rhythm groups, and every root in her transcriptions is stressed on its last non-echo syllable. Neither source gives an explicit placement rule for Apinayé; Salanova's explicit 'underlyingly final' statement is about Mebengokre (p. 21). A minor internal wrinkle: both sources occasionally transcribe stress on the echo vowel itself (Ham [ka'tu·'di͜I] 'shoulder'; Salanova (98d) [pʌ̃ˈmʌ] 'father').

sources.citation: Callow, John Campbell. 1962. The Apinayé language: phonology and grammar. PhD thesis, SOAS, University of London. iv+154 pp. (etnolinguistica.org scan, 312 pp.)
sources.quote: "There is only one prosodic feature, stress, which is set up as a prosodic feature for the whole word ... In the simple word in isolation, the (ultimate) syllable-unit S always occurs with primary stress; the penultimate syllable unit U with tertiary stress; and the antepenultimate syllable unit U with secondary stress." Syllable unit S "occurs word-final and with primary stress, whereas the syllable unit U never occurs word-final". In repetitive (reduplicated) words "the second syllable unit S carries primary stress" (e.g. katotok 'thunder' (kadot'tog)).

sources.quote: "Na língua apinayé, cada palavra de mais de uma sílaba possui um acento de liberdade limitada, que pode recair nas duas últimas sílabas da palavra. Ressaltamos, entretanto, que na maioria das palavras da língua Apinayé, o acento recai na última sílaba." Lists (a) paroxítonas: jàtxore [ʒatˈtʃorɛ] 'mamãozinho', xore [ˈtʃorɛ] 'raposa', tyini [ˈtɨjdi] 'avó', tyjre 'avozinha', katõtõk 'trovão' ...; (b) oxítonas: mãti [mãˈdi] 'ema', kagô [kaˈŋgo] 'suco', karà [kaˈrʌ] 'veado', paaxi [paaˈtʃi] 'melancia' etc. No rule is given for when penultimate stress occurs; several paroxytone items are diminutives
